6145.title: Play Space
6145.heading: Play Space
6145.content:
Play space is the set of states and traversable paths made possible by a game's tokens, rules, and systems. It is the possibility space within which players choose actions and pursue goals.

A broad play space contains several viable routes whose consequences differ. A dominant strategy or heavily scripted path collapses that space, reducing [[Meaningful Decision|meaningful decisions]], engagement, and replay value.

Platform-genre fit is the relationship between a game's dominant challenges and the capabilities and use context of its target machine. A genre works well when the platform's input, display, performance, network, physical setting, and session pattern support its central actions.

Fit is not a permanent rule, but adapting a mismatch has costs. A design should explain how it replaces missing controls, preserves essential information, and suits the audience's likely environment.

6160.title: Planning Poker
6160.heading: Planning Poker
6160.content:
Planning Poker is a group estimation technique in which participants reveal estimates simultaneously, then discuss the assumptions behind the largest differences. The group repeats the process until it reaches enough shared understanding to choose an estimate.

Simultaneous revelation limits anchoring by the first or most senior speaker. The valuable output is often the conversation that exposes different interpretations, risks, and implementation knowledge.

6163.title: Plane Stress
6163.heading: Plane Stress
6163.content:
Plane stress is a two-dimensional idealization for thin, flat bodies loaded within their plane. Stress components normal to the plane and transverse shear stresses are assumed negligible.

The in-plane displacement field still varies over the surface, and the constitutive matrix is specialized to the plane-stress assumption. Thickness enters element force and stiffness calculations even though out-of-plane stress is omitted.

6166.title: Plane Strain
6166.heading: Plane Strain
6166.content:
Plane strain is a two-dimensional idealization in which out-of-plane strain components are constrained to zero. It is appropriate for bodies whose geometry and loading vary little along a long constrained direction.

Plane strain and plane stress use similar mesh procedures but different constitutive matrices. Choosing between them changes the relationship among in-plane stress, strain, and Poisson effects.

6169.title: Plane Specification
6169.heading: Plane Specification
6169.content:
Plane specification identifies a flat surface in the physical environment for modeling or content placement. The plane can be derived from several measured points, fitted to observed data, or selected from reconstructed geometry.

Once established, it supplies a position, orientation, and two-dimensional surface coordinate system. Augmentations can then be constrained to a wall, floor, tabletop, or planar object rather than positioned freely in space.

6172.sourceSearchName: plane and surface geometry plane and surface geometry
6172.title: Plane and Surface Geometry
6172.heading: Plane and Surface Geometry
6172.content:
A plane is a flat two-dimensional set extending through three-dimensional space, while a surface is a two-dimensional boundary that may curve. Planes often provide construction frames or idealized domains; surfaces enclose solids, define interfaces, and carry boundary conditions.

Three non-collinear points are sufficient to define a plane. A usable surface model additionally requires consistent connectivity and orientation so that the analysis tool can distinguish adjoining regions and, when appropriate, infer an enclosed volume.

6173.title: Plane and Surface Geometry
6173.heading: References

6175.title: Plane Geometry
6175.heading: Plane Geometry
6175.content:
A plane in game collision geometry is represented by a normalized surface normal and a signed distance from the origin. Substituting a point into the plane equation determines which side of the plane contains it and how far away it lies.

The normal also supplies the orientation needed for reflection and collision response. Line and segment intersection solves for the parameter at which their points satisfy the plane equation.

6178.title: Plane Equation in Three Dimensions
6178.heading: Plane Equation in Three Dimensions
6178.content:
A plane with normal vector $n=(a,b,c)$ through $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ consists of points satisfying

$$a(x-x_0)+b(y-y_0)+c(z-z_0)=0.$$

Equivalently, it has equation $ax+by+cz=d$. The normal vector is perpendicular to every displacement vector lying in the plane.

6184.title: Planar Process
6184.heading: Planar Process
6184.content:
Jean Hoerni’s planar process fabricated flat silicon transistors beneath a protective oxide surface. The geometry allowed devices and their interconnections to be patterned across a wafer.

This manufacturing method made Robert Noyce’s integrated-circuit design practical. It became a foundation of modern semiconductor production.

6187.sourceSearchName: planar perspective rectification planar perspective rectification
6187.title: Planar Perspective Rectification
6187.heading: Planar Perspective Rectification
6187.content:
Planar perspective rectification transforms an oblique view of a flat surface into a front-facing view by estimating the plane's projective geometry. Parallel lines, right angles, or known shapes can supply the constraints needed to compute the transformation.

Rectification can make signs, documents, license plates, and other planar details easier to inspect. It reorganizes sampled information but cannot recover detail that blur, occlusion, or insufficient resolution never recorded; enhancement should not be mistaken for reconstruction of lost evidence.

6190.title: Plaintext and Ciphertext
6190.heading: Plaintext and Ciphertext
6190.content:
Plaintext is the original readable input to an encryption process, while ciphertext is the scrambled output intended to conceal that meaning. Plaintext may represent text, images, audio, video, or other digital data rather than only written words.

[[Encryption]] combines plaintext with an [[Encryption Key]] to produce ciphertext, and decryption combines ciphertext with the appropriate key to recover plaintext. Security depends on the transformation and key, not on ciphertext merely looking unfamiliar.

6193.title: Piranha CMS
6193.heading: Piranha CMS
6193.content:
Piranha CMS is a .NET content-management framework designed to integrate with ASP.NET Core applications. It supplies content APIs and a manager interface while allowing developers to define the application's content structures and rendering behavior.

The framework can manage sites, pages, posts, media, and reusable content components. Because it participates in the surrounding ASP.NET Core application, routing, dependency injection, persistence, and authorization remain part of the overall design.

6196.heading: Pin Fin Geometry
6196.content:
A pin fin is a slender extended surface, commonly built from a circular cross section extruded or represented by a cylinder. Its defining parameters include diameter or radius, height, placement, and the geometry of its attachment to a base.

Repeated pin arrangements can be generated with array transforms, but spacing becomes part of the physical model when neighboring thermal or flow fields interact. Measurements of volume and exposed area support comparisons with other fin forms.

6198.heading: Document

6199.sourceSearchName: pipes and filters architecture pipes and filters architecture
6199.title: Pipes-and-Filters Architecture
6199.heading: Pipes-and-Filters Architecture
6199.content:
A pipes-and-filters architecture divides processing into independent filters connected by data-carrying pipes. Each filter transforms its inputs into outputs without needing to own the entire augmented-reality application.

Tracking, calibration, fusion, and rendering stages can be composed and tested in isolation, and a pipe can cross a network boundary in a distributed system. The interfaces must retain timing, coordinate, and type information needed by downstream components.

6202.title: Pipeline Trigger
6202.heading: Pipeline Trigger
6202.content:
A pipeline trigger is the event that starts an automated pipeline. A source-code change can trigger continuous integration so the shared repository is compiled and tested without waiting for someone to launch the build manually.

Trigger scope determines which branches or changes receive that feedback. It should align with the repository flow that the team considers eligible for integration or release.

6205.sourceSearchName: pinhole camera model pinhole camera model
6205.title: Pinhole Camera Model
6205.heading: Pinhole Camera Model
6205.content:
The pinhole camera model represents a camera as a center of projection and a flat image plane separated by a focal length. Light from each scene point travels through the center to one sensor location, producing a compact geometric account of image formation.

Real lenses introduce distortion, blur, and other effects, but the model captures the perspective relationships needed by many forensic tests. It provides the common foundation for [[Vanishing Point]] analysis, scene reconstruction, and reasoning about apparent scale.

6217.title: Pig Latin
6217.heading: Pig Latin
6217.content:
Pig Latin is the procedural dataflow language used by [[Apache Pig]]. Each statement applies a transformation to relations made from bags, tuples, and fields, allowing a pipeline to load, filter, group, order, and store large datasets.

The compiler converts the script into logical and physical operator plans and then into MapReduce jobs. Its concise syntax improves expressiveness, but external control flow is normally needed for iterative algorithms.

6220.heading: Piecewise-Defined Function
6220.content: A piecewise-defined function uses different formulas on specified portions of its domain. Endpoint inequalities determine which rule supplies a boundary value. This form can represent thresholds and abrupt changes, and it makes comparison of left- and right-hand behavior explicit when studying [[Continuity at a Point]] and [[One-Sided Limit]]s.

6223.title: Pie Chart
6223.heading: Pie Chart
6223.content:
A pie chart represents category proportions as angles or areas of a circle. It is frequently requested for categorical summaries, but people compare angles and areas less accurately than positions along a common scale.

Small categories also produce crowded labels and nearly invisible slices. A [[Bar Chart]] is usually easier to read, while a legend may be required when the pie must be used despite these limitations.

6229.content:
Physiological pulse signal detection measures tiny periodic facial-color changes caused by blood circulation. By tracking a face through video and combining subtle temporal variations, an analysis can recover a pulse-like signal that is normally invisible to direct viewing.

A rendered or synthesized face may lack this living physiological rhythm even when its appearance and motion seem realistic. The cue is not permanent protection against fakery: motion, illumination, compression, and skin visibility affect measurement, and a generator can be modified to reproduce a plausible signal.

Tracked props and tangible objects can provide shape, weight, contact, and shared access without simulating those qualities visually. The digital mapping should respect the physical behavior closely enough that the combined object remains understandable.

6244.heading: Physical Map
6244.content: A physical map depicts landscape and natural features such as terrain, water, and relief. [[Hill Shading]] can make landform visible, but every layer must share compatible coordinates and an intentional visual hierarchy. 6247.heading: Physical Layer
6247.content:
The physical layer carries raw bits as electrical, optical, or radio signals over a medium. It concerns the mechanics and signaling needed for a device to place bits on a channel and receive them from that channel.

Higher layers can describe frames, addresses, and protocols only after this layer supplies an actual transmission path. Signal strength and the characteristics of the medium can therefore affect integrity and throughput above it.

6250.sourceSearchName: physical input layer physical input layer
6250.title: Physical Input Layer
6250.heading: Physical Input Layer
6250.content:
The physical input layer is the bodily action and [[Input Device|input mechanism]] through which a player performs a [[Game Verb]]. A digital action may be represented onscreen, but the player actually presses, holds, releases, points, swipes, or moves a control.

Different inputs provide different degrees and rhythms of control. A binary key suits discrete grid movement, while a mouse supports continuous motion on two axes. The design should use the properties of its input method and make the physical performance reinforce the pace and character of the represented verb.

6253.heading: Physical Game Prototype
6253.content:
A physical game prototype enacts movement, timing, spatial relationships, or social coordination with bodies and ordinary objects. It investigates how an interaction feels before its digital implementation is available.

The prototype abstracts away technology while preserving the relationship under study. Its value comes from testing embodied pacing and roles, not from accurately reproducing every eventual rule or visual detail.

6256.title: Physical Ergonomics
6256.heading: Physical Ergonomics
6256.content:
Physical ergonomics concerns how the human musculoskeletal system affects safe, comfortable, and effective interaction. Relevant factors include posture, reach, grip, device weight and balance, muscle groups, movement range, repetition, and how long a pose must be held.

An interaction can be accurate in a short test yet become tiring or painful during realistic use. A device should therefore be evaluated with representative tasks, grips, poses, and durations. In handheld systems, balance and control placement may matter as much as total weight.

Physical ergonomics is a major part of [[Human Factors]] and contributes directly to [[Usability]].

6259.content:
The physical dimension of a game world defines its simulated space, including dimensionality, scale, boundaries, and the relative size and speed of objects. These properties determine where entities can move and what spatial actions are possible.

Physical design may distort real proportions or travel times to serve play. The important requirement is internal clarity: players must be able to build a reliable model of reach, movement, obstruction, and distance.

6265.heading: Physical Basis of Digital Information
6265.content:
Digital information always depends on a physical arrangement capable of carrying distinguishable states. Signals in circuits and changes in storage media provide the material events that designers interpret as bits, data, and instructions.

Programs may be described abstractly, but execution requires physical mechanisms with timing, energy, noise, and failure constraints. Ignoring that substrate can hide causes of faults that are invisible at the software level.

6268.heading: Physical Attack on GPS Infrastructure
6268.content: A physical attack on GPS infrastructure could target spacecraft, control facilities, tracking stations, or communication links. Medium-Earth-orbit satellites are harder to reach than low-orbit vehicles, and constellation spares mean that disabling one satellite does not disable the service. Secured and redundant control sites add another layer. These measures raise the cost and visibility of an attack, but they do not make a global system invulnerable.

6271.title: Physical and Temporal Separation
6271.heading: Physical and Temporal Separation
6271.content:
Physical separation assigns sensitive work to different hardware, creating a strong boundary because the activities do not share the same machine. Its equipment and coordination costs make it impractical for many ordinary applications.

Temporal separation reuses hardware but schedules protected tasks at different times. It reduces simultaneous interference while relying on the system to clear or protect state left behind between execution periods.

6274.sourceSearchName: phrase based text feature phrase based text feature
6274.title: Phrase-Based Text Feature
6274.heading: Phrase-Based Text Feature
6274.content:
A phrase-based text feature uses a multiword unit rather than a single token. Syntactic phrases, head-modifier pairs, adjacent n-grams, or statistically associated word combinations can distinguish meanings that bags of individual words collapse.

Greater specificity improves discrimination but reduces coverage because long combinations occur less often. Phrase features are therefore commonly added to single-word features, which retain broad coverage and reduce overfitting. Non-compositional expressions may instead need treatment as indivisible units.

6277.title: Photovoltaic Effect
6277.heading: Photovoltaic Effect
6277.content: The photovoltaic effect converts incident light directly into electrical output in a semiconductor junction. Absorbed [[Photon Energy]] creates electron-hole pairs; the field of a [[P-N Junction]] drives their charge carriers apart, allowing an external load to receive current. No steam, gas turbine, or rotating generator lies between sunlight and this cell-level electrical conversion, although a practical [[Solar Array]] still needs supporting equipment.

6279.sourceSearchName: photovoltaic battery capacity photovoltaic battery capacity
6279.title: Photovoltaic Battery Capacity
6279.heading: Document

6280.sourceSearchName: photovoltaic battery capacity photovoltaic battery capacity
6280.title: Photovoltaic Battery Capacity
6280.heading: Photovoltaic Battery Capacity
6280.content: Battery capacity in an [[Autonomous Photovoltaic Plant]] must cover demand during a chosen number of low-sun days without exceeding allowable discharge depth. The source's sizing inputs are daily load, reserve factor, autonomy days, battery voltage, discharge limit, and efficiency. A battery's rated ampere-hours alone do not describe usable delivered energy, because charging and discharging incur losses.

6281.sourceSearchName: photovoltaic battery capacity photovoltaic battery capacity

6281.heading: References

6282.sourceSearchName: photovoltaic array sizing photovoltaic array sizing

6282.heading: Document

6283.sourceSearchName: photovoltaic array sizing photovoltaic array sizing
6283.title: Photovoltaic Array Sizing
6283.heading: Photovoltaic Array Sizing
6283.content: Array sizing matches expected electrical load to site sunlight and generator efficiency. The source first sums each consumer's power multiplied by daily operating hours, then uses daily radiation and photovoltaic efficiency to estimate required [[Solar Array]] area and module count. Ambient temperature, network voltage, storage specification, and standby supply also affect the design; a peak-watt module rating alone is insufficient.

6284.sourceSearchName: photovoltaic array sizing photovoltaic array sizing
6284.title: Photovoltaic Array Sizing
6284.heading: References

6286.title: Photon Flux
6286.heading: Photon Flux
6286.content: Photon flux counts photons crossing a surface perpendicular to a light beam per unit area and time. When average [[Photon Energy]] is known, radiant power per area is photon flux multiplied by that energy. In a solar cell, more photons able to form charge carriers can raise current, but flux alone says nothing about how much of the spectrum the junction can use.

6289.title: Photon Energy
6289.heading: Photon Energy
6289.content: A photon carries a discrete amount of radiant energy. Its energy rises with frequency and falls with wavelength: $E=h\nu=hc/\lambda$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $\nu$ is frequency, $c$ is light speed, and $\lambda$ is wavelength. In a [[Photovoltaic Effect]], the photon must provide enough energy to promote an electron across the material's [[Semiconductor Band Gap]].

6292.heading: Photometric Unit Conversion by Area
6292.content: Photometric quantities in the book include luminous intensity, flux, luminance, and illuminance, each with a different unit expression. Luminance can be given in cd/in² or cd/m², while illuminance can be given in footcandles or lux. In both of its displayed examples the area lies in the denominator, so converting square inches or square feet requires an inverse area factor. The illuminance example gives about 10.76 lux per footcandle. See [[Area Unit Scaling]] and [[Algebraic SI Derived Units]].

6295.title: Photometric Registration
6295.heading: Photometric Registration
6295.content:
Photometric registration aligns the lighting and appearance of virtual content with the physical scene. It estimates relevant illumination, material, exposure, and color relationships so generated objects respond to light in a manner compatible with the captured image.

Geometric alignment can place an object correctly while inconsistent brightness, shadow direction, or reflection still exposes it as synthetic. Photometric registration supplies the information needed for common illumination and coherent compositing.

6298.heading: Photolithography in Chip Fabrication
6298.content:
Photolithography transfers miniature circuit patterns onto a semiconductor wafer using light-sensitive materials and controlled exposure. Successive steps define doped regions, conductors, and other device features.

The technique scales circuits by printing them rather than wiring each component by hand. It made dense, repeatable, mass-produced integrated circuits practical.

6301.title: Photoelectric Effect
6301.heading: Photoelectric Effect
6301.content: The photoelectric effect emits electrons from a material when incident radiation exceeds a threshold frequency. Einstein modeled the light as photons of energy $hf$, giving maximum electron kinetic energy $K_{max}=hf-\phi$. Frequency controls electron energy, while intensity above threshold primarily controls the number of emitted electrons.

6304.sourceSearchName: photo response non uniformity photo response non uniformity
6304.title: Photo-Response Non-Uniformity
6304.heading: Photo-Response Non-Uniformity
6304.content:
Photo-response non-uniformity is the stable, pixel-by-pixel variation in a sensor's sensitivity to light. Manufacturing differences cause nominally identical elements to respond slightly differently, producing a weak pattern proportional to scene brightness.

The pattern is largely unique to one physical sensor, even among cameras of the same model. Estimating it reliably usually requires averaging noise residuals from roughly ten to twenty suitable, evenly illuminated images so scene content and random noise cancel.

6307.title: Phosphoric Acid Fuel Cell
6307.heading: Phosphoric Acid Fuel Cell
6307.content: A phosphoric acid fuel cell uses phosphoric acid as its [[Fuel Cell Electrolyte]] and operates at a higher temperature than a polymer-membrane cell. The source presents it for buildings, small power plants, and combined heat-and-power supply. Electricity-only efficiency and total useful-energy efficiency are distinct: reclaiming its heat raises the latter, but does not turn that heat into extra electrical output.

6309.heading: Document

6310.sourceSearchName: phong reflection model phong reflection model
6310.title: Phong Reflection Model
6310.heading: Phong Reflection Model
6310.content:
The Phong reflection model approximates surface lighting by combining ambient, diffuse, and specular contributions. Diffuse response depends on the angle between light and surface normal, while the specular term produces a view-dependent highlight.

It is a bidirectional reflectance model used to calculate how lights affect an object. Its components are efficient enough for real-time use but simplify the physical behavior of light.

6311.sourceSearchName: phong reflection model phong reflection model
6311.title: Phong Reflection Model
6311.heading: References

6313.title: Phonetic Transcription
6313.heading: Phonetic Transcription
6313.content:
Phonetic transcription maps normalized words to a sequence of speech sounds for synthesis. It must handle ordinary vocabulary, names, abbreviations, and words whose pronunciation depends on context.

The transcription guides the [[Speech Synthesizer]] in producing the segmental content of the utterance. Prosodic choices such as [[Intonation]] determine how those sounds unfold over time.

6316.title: Phoneme
6316.heading: Phoneme
6316.content:
A phoneme is a language-specific sound category that can distinguish words. Actual pronunciations vary, but phoneme sequences provide an intermediate representation between written words and acoustic observations.

A [[Pronunciation Model]] maps a word to one or more phoneme sequences. The [[Acoustic Model]] then estimates how well observed speech matches those sound units.

6319.title: Phenomenological Thinking
6319.heading: Phenomenological Thinking
6319.content:
Phenomenological thinking treats observed events as separate phenomena without necessarily looking for a deeper structure connecting them. It is useful for noticing what occurs, but it can miss the interactions and loops that produce recurring behavior.

When an apparent event is an expression of a [[System]], a purely phenomenological view may address symptoms rather than causes. [[Systems Thinking]] extends observation by asking how parts and feedback generate the phenomenon.

6321.sourceSearchName: perspective n point problem perspective n point problem
6321.title: Perspective-n-Point Problem
6321.heading: Document

6322.sourceSearchName: perspective n point problem perspective n point problem
6322.title: Perspective-n-Point Problem
6322.heading: Perspective-n-Point Problem
6322.content:
The perspective-n-point problem determines a calibrated camera's pose from correspondences between known three-dimensional points and their two-dimensional image projections. The unknown rotation and translation must explain how the model points appear in the image.

Natural-feature tracking uses a PnP solution after descriptor matching. Because some correspondences may be wrong, the solver is commonly placed inside a robust sampling process and followed by pose refinement.

6323.sourceSearchName: perspective n point problem perspective n point problem
6323.title: Perspective-n-Point Problem
6323.heading: References

6325.title: Perspective Projection
6325.heading: Perspective Projection
6325.content:
Perspective projection maps a three-dimensional scene point onto a two-dimensional sensor along a ray through the camera center. In the pinhole model, image position is proportional to focal length and lateral scene position and inversely proportional to depth.

The relation explains why nearby objects appear larger and why parallel scene lines may converge in an image. Photogrammetric forensic methods use these invariants to test whether objects, shadows, reflections, and camera parameters could belong to one coherent scene.

6328.sourceSearchName: personally identifiable information personally identifiable information
6328.title: Personally Identifiable Information
6328.heading: Personally Identifiable Information
6328.content:
Personally identifiable information is information that can distinguish or trace an individual's identity or that is linked or linkable to that individual. Examples include identity numbers, birth details, biometric records, and medical, educational, financial, or employment information.

A collection can become identifying through combination even when one field appears harmless in isolation. Cloud services handling this information need explicit privacy, access, retention, transmission, location, and deletion rules.

6331.title: Personalized Advertising
6331.heading: Personalized Advertising
6331.content:
Personalized advertising selects messages using information about an individual's behavior, characteristics, or inferred interests. Mobile and cross-platform records let advertisers tailor content more closely than broad audience categories allow.

Personalization can increase relevance, but it also depends on tracking and data exchange that consumers may not understand. The privacy issue concerns the full profile and reuse pathway, not only the final advertisement shown.

6333.sourceSearchName: personal virtual assistant personal virtual assistant
6333.title: Personal Virtual Assistant
6333.heading: Document

6334.sourceSearchName: personal virtual assistant personal virtual assistant
6334.title: Personal Virtual Assistant
6334.heading: Personal Virtual Assistant
6334.content:
A personal virtual assistant serves one user across many domains and devices. It can answer questions, manage personal information, invoke services, and use [[Personal Context]] to tailor results.

Its breadth creates a triggering problem: the system must infer which [[Assistant Skill]] should handle an utterance before that skill can interpret the request in detail.

6335.sourceSearchName: personal virtual assistant personal virtual assistant
6335.title: Personal Virtual Assistant
6335.heading: References

6337.title: Personal Iteration
6337.heading: Personal Iteration
6337.content:
Personal iteration is the local loop in which a developer changes code or content, runs it, observes the result, and revises it. Hardware speed, build tools, in-game editing, and asset hot loading determine how frequently this loop can occur.

Reducing seconds or minutes from a loop repeated throughout the day compounds into more experiments and earlier discovery of defects or design problems.

6340.sourceSearchName: personal health device data personal health device data
6340.title: Personal Health Device Data
6340.heading: Personal Health Device Data
6340.content:
Personal health device data are measurements produced by consumer or personal-use healthcare terminals and sensors. They can extend observation beyond institutions and provide frequent records of activity or physiological state.

Device accuracy, user behavior, changing hardware, and incomplete context affect interpretation. Continuous collection also creates privacy and governance questions because intimate information may flow through commercial systems.

6341.title: Personal Health Device Data

6342.title: Personal Health Cloud
6342.heading: Document

6343.sourceSearchName: personal health cloud personal health cloud
6343.title: Personal Health Cloud
6343.heading: Personal Health Cloud
6343.content:
A personal health cloud stores and organizes one person's health records and measurements across devices and services. Wearables or home sensors can contribute measurements such as weight, heart rate, or blood pressure, while authorized people can receive selected information.

Automated monitoring can alert the person, family, or clinician when a threshold is crossed. Because the data is personal and sensitive, consent, access, retention, location, and the uncertainty of predictions must be explicit.

6346.heading: Personal Digital Assistant
6346.content:
A personal digital assistant is a handheld computer organized around personal information such as contacts, appointments, notes, and tasks. It emphasizes quick interaction, portability, and synchronization rather than desktop-scale software.

PDAs created a bridge between organizers and mobile phones. Their interface and application ideas survived even after smartphones absorbed the category.

6349.title: Personal Data
6349.heading: Personal Data
6349.content:
Personal data is any information that relates to an identified or identifiable natural person. The definition reaches beyond names and direct identifiers: a record can become personal when it can be connected to someone through available means or combined with other information.

In big-data systems, identifiability is contextual. Seemingly anonymous observations may reveal a person through patterns, linkage, or inference, so governance must examine the complete processing environment rather than each field in isolation.

The legal distinction between personal and anonymous data is therefore better understood as a scale than as a permanent binary. Information can move toward identifiability when it is combined with other records or analyzed with stronger techniques.
links: Big Data Law and Individual Rights

6350.title: Personal Data
6350.heading: References
links: Big Data Law and Individual Rights

6352.title: Personal Context
6352.heading: Personal Context
6352.content:
Personal context is information about the user that can help an assistant interpret or rank possible actions. It may include preferences, location, contacts, calendar state, past choices, or device settings.

A [[Personal Virtual Assistant]] can use this context in [[Candidate Hypothesis Ranking]] and response generation. Because it can reveal sensitive behavior, access and retention must match the user's privacy expectations.

6354.sourceSearchName: personal computer ownership model personal computer ownership model
6354.title: Personal Computer Ownership Model
6354.heading: Document

6355.sourceSearchName: personal computer ownership model personal computer ownership model
6355.title: Personal Computer Ownership Model
6355.heading: Personal Computer Ownership Model
6355.content:
The personal-computer model gives an individual direct control over a machine rather than allocating brief access through a shared mainframe. Owners can experiment, customize, play games, and run interactive applications without an operator’s permission.

This desire was underestimated by advocates of time-sharing utilities. Falling semiconductor costs and hobbyist culture made ownership practical and socially compelling.

6358.sourceSearchName: personal computer game platform personal computer game platform
6358.title: Personal Computer Game Platform
6358.heading: Personal Computer Game Platform
6358.content:
The personal computer is a flexible game platform used at a desk by one person, with keyboard, mouse, display, storage, networking, and hardware configurations that vary widely. It supports detailed interfaces, modification, and many genres.

Variation is both strength and cost. Designers gain precision controls and extensibility but must account for performance ranges, installation environments, display differences, and a less standardized input setup.

6359.title: Personal Computer Game Platform
6359.heading: References

6361.title: Personal Cloud
6361.heading: Personal Cloud
6361.content:
A personal cloud is a cloud whose scope is one person and that person's information or activities. It can store documents, media, financial information, shopping preferences, or health records and make them available across locations and devices.

The scope does not determine the deployment model: a personal cloud can be private, public, or hybrid. As it combines more intimate data and services, ownership, consent, provider access, interoperability, and security become especially important.

6364.title: Persistent World
6364.heading: Persistent World
6364.content:
A persistent world is a large online game world with no single beginning or ending that continues while individual players join, act, and leave. State and community outlast any one session.

Persistence creates ongoing design and service obligations: economies evolve, new and veteran players coexist, content is consumed, social norms develop, and operators must maintain security and support.

6367.title: Persistent Connection
6367.heading: Persistent Connection
6367.content:
A persistent connection remains available across multiple messages instead of ending after one request-response exchange. SignalR manages this ongoing communication channel and chooses suitable transport behavior for the client and server environment.

Because the channel has a lifetime, connection state becomes part of application behavior. Startup, disconnection, retry, and cleanup must be considered alongside the messages themselves.

6369.heading: Document

6370.sourceSearchName: persistent blender handlers persistent blender handlers
6370.title: Persistent Blender Handlers
6370.heading: Persistent Blender Handlers
6370.content:
Ordinary Blender application handlers are cleared when another `.blend` file is loaded. Decorating a handler as persistent tells Blender to retain it across that file transition, which is necessary for callbacks intended to run after each load.

Persistence should be intentional because the callback continues to affect later scenes. A persistent load handler can print diagnostics or restore behavior, but it must not assume that objects from the previous file still exist. Its body should discover the new scene's data when invoked and its add-on should still provide a way to unregister it.

6373.title: Persistence Impedance Mismatch
6373.heading: Persistence Impedance Mismatch
6373.content: Persistence impedance mismatch is the tension between a domain object's natural structure and the shapes or construction rules required by a storage system. A document database may require a string identity or serializer-friendly constructor, while a relational database maps object composition into tables and foreign keys. An object-relational mapper reduces some mechanical work but does not remove the mismatch. The model should keep storage compromises explicit so persistence concerns do not quietly turn a [[Domain Model]] into an [[Anemic Domain Model]].

6376.title: Perpendicular Bisector
6376.heading: Perpendicular Bisector
6376.content: The perpendicular bisector of a segment passes through its midpoint and meets the segment at a right angle. In coordinates, first average the endpoint coordinates to find the midpoint, then use a perpendicular slope to construct its line equation. Every point on this bisector is equidistant from the two endpoints.

6379.title: Permutation Test
6379.heading: Permutation Test
6379.content:
A permutation test approximates a [[Null Distribution]] by repeatedly shuffling group labels and recalculating the statistic. If labels are exchangeable under the null, these rearrangements represent results that could occur without a group effect.

The procedure is useful when a standard analytical approximation is unavailable or doubtful. Its validity depends on the randomization structure, while the number of permutations determines the resolution and Monte Carlo error of the estimated tail probability.

6382.title: Permutation
6382.heading: Permutation
6382.content:
A permutation is a rearrangement of a collection's elements into a different order. The elements themselves and their multiplicities remain unchanged.

The result of a [[Sorting Algorithm]] must be a permutation of its input. Ordering the records correctly is not sufficient if an item is lost, duplicated, or altered during the process.

6385.title: Permutation Matrix
6385.heading: Permutation Matrix
6385.content:
A permutation matrix contains only zeros and ones, with exactly one one in each row and each column. Left multiplication permutes rows; right multiplication permutes columns.

Pivoting can therefore be recorded algebraically with a permutation matrix. An LU factorization with row exchanges is commonly expressed as $PA=LU$.

6388.title: Permutation Group
6388.heading: Permutation Group
6388.content:
A permutation group is a group whose elements are bijections of a set and whose operation is function composition. Every group is isomorphic to a permutation group acting on its own elements.

Cycle notation makes finite permutations and their composition more compact.

6391.title: Performative and Expressive Play
6391.heading: Performative and Expressive Play
6391.content:
Performative play turns playing into an act for an audience, whether spectators are physically present, online, or represented by other participants. Expressive play lets players communicate identity, style, feeling, or authorship through choices inside the system.

The two forms can overlap without being identical. A private customization can be expressive without an audience, while a public feat can be performative even when it offers little personal authorship.

6394.title: Perceptual Symbol Scaling
6394.heading: Perceptual Symbol Scaling
6394.content: Perceptual symbol scaling adjusts mathematically proportional areas to compensate for systematic human underestimation of differences between symbol sizes. It can make magnitude changes more visually apparent than uncorrected [[Symbol Area Scaling]]. The correction is an empirical viewing model, not a change in the data, so the legend should display actual example values. Excessive correction can overstate differences just as badly as uncorrected radius scaling.

6397.title: Performance-Guided Feature Search
6397.heading: Performance-Guided Feature Search
6397.content:
Performance-guided feature search uses measured or predicted task performance to decide which transformations to explore next. Each evaluation supplies feedback about a derived dataset's utility.

Direct model training gives relevant evidence but is expensive and can overfit repeated validation. Surrogate scores, careful holdout design, and budget-aware policies reduce that cost and bias.

6400.title: Performance-Based Pricing
6400.heading: Performance-Based Pricing
6400.content:
Performance-based pricing ties part of a service's charge to a measurable benchmark or result. The metric should have a clear connection to a business process or outcome so that the payment encourages behavior valuable to the consumer.

The approach can align provider and consumer goals, but attributing an outcome to the cloud service may be difficult. [[Outcome-Based Pricing]], [[Business-Linked Pricing]], and [[Gain-Share Pricing]] use different forms of that relationship.
